pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), META. Use place-value understanding AND known number facts together to solve problems: knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and a bond like 3+2=5 lets you reason 34 + 20 = 54, or work backwards ('add 10 to my number and I get 45'). This is the application layer that turns tens-and-ones knowledge into a problem-solving tool.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'use place value and number facts to solve problems'; recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4/5/6 and 2.NBT.5–9 — add/subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations; mentally find 10 more/less.
• Operational details — Keep it strategy-based, not algorithm-based at this stage: partition (34 = 30 + 4), operate on the parts, recombine. Model missing-number and 'I think of a number' problems that demand working backwards. Emphasise that a known fact (3+2) plus place value (these are TENS) generates a new fact (30+20). Use concrete/pictorial support and expect children to explain WHICH fact and WHICH partition they used.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use 34 = 30 + 4 to add a multiple of ten (34 + 20) with blocks. Tier B (age 6-7): solve a one-step missing-number problem ('__ + 10 = 45') by reasoning about the tens. Tier C (age 7): solve a two-step or unfamiliar-context problem, choosing a partition and a known fact, and explain the reasoning.
bestPractices: Teach partition–operate–recombine explicitly: split into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, put it back together — making the place-value structure the engine of the strategy.
Connect a known bond to its place-value scaling out loud: 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50' — so number facts and place value are used together, not in isolation.
Use missing-number and 'think of a number' problems to force flexible, backwards reasoning rather than one-directional calculation.
Insist on explanation/justification ('which fact did you use? how did you split it?') so the META goal — choosing and applying structure — is assessed, not just the answer.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram splitting a number into tens and ones
Empty/marked number line for jumps of tens and ones
Bar model for missing-number and comparison problems
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a counting-in-ones or column method instead of using place-value structure, because the number-fact link was never made.
Applying a known bond but forgetting the unit — saying 30 + 20 = 5 (using 3+2 but dropping the tens).
Unable to work backwards — treating 'think of a number' problems as if they can only be solved forwards.
Partitioning incorrectly under a problem's wording (mis-splitting 34 as 3 + 4 rather than 30 + 4).
Focusing on getting an answer without checking it fits the problem, so an unreasonable result goes unquestioned.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2), help children use place-value structure together with known number facts to solve problems — e.g. knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and 3 + 2 = 5 to reason that 34 + 20 = 54, and to work backwards on 'I think of a number' problems. The core strategy is partition–operate–recombine: split a number into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, then put it back together, saying aloud which fact and which partition were used. Keep it strategy-based (not column algorithm) at this stage, support with concrete and pictorial models, and insist on explanation so the META goal — choosing and justifying structure — is what develops.

activities.title: Problem playground: partition, operate, recombine
feedback: If the child counts all 54 from one, prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' and show the shortcut (30 + 20) beside the count rather than reteaching the bonds.

If the child refuses to attempt because 'we haven't done this one', think aloud how a known fact generates a new one, name derivation as real mathematics, and invite them to build the next step themselves.
If they say 30 + 20 = 5, point back to the blocks: these are tens, so the answer is 50, not 5 — the unit must be kept.
If they split 34 as 3 + 4, re-anchor on the part-whole diagram: the 3 stands for 30 (three tens).
For the work-backwards mode, if they treat it as only solvable forwards, invite them to test a value and check whether '+10' lands on 45, adjusting up or down.
activities.rationale: Making partition–operate–recombine visible and generative lets the place-value structure act as the engine of the strategy; auto-generating fresh problems supports transfer, and a work-backwards mode forces flexible reasoning. Linked fact-chains and live recombination (e.g. a fact ribbon lighting up, number-line testing) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Take a problem such as 34 + 20 and split 34 into a 30-part and a 4-part (using base-ten blocks, a part-whole 'cherry' diagram, or drawing).
Add the 20 onto the tens part only, saying aloud 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50'.
Recombine the parts: 50 + 4 = 54, and state the full chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54.
Try a 'mystery number' / work-backwards problem such as '__ + 10 = 45': cover or guess the start number and test candidate values on a number line until the equation holds.
Repeat with fresh problems (e.g. 34 + 30, 56 + 20) so the strategy — not one answer — is what transfers.
activities.intendedInsight: A number bond you already own (like 3 + 2) can do the heavy lifting on tens, so an unfamiliar calculation can be derived by partitioning and recruiting a known fact rather than counted out from one.

activities.title: Socratic coaching: which fact and which split?
feedback: If the child reverts to counting, nudge toward place value: 'what known fact is hiding in here?'
If they cannot say why splitting 34 into 30 and 4 is legitimate, revisit the part-whole model to show the whole is unchanged.
Affirm reasoning that names both the partition and the fact, even if the final arithmetic needs a small correction.
activities.rationale: Because this is a META skill about choosing and justifying, dialogue that asks the child to state and defend a method can develop the reasoning and respond to the child's chosen approach. This is offered as one effective format alongside hands-on work, not as the only way to teach justification.
sourceClaims: Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Face a posed problem (e.g. 34 + 20 or a two-step unfamiliar-context problem) and explain the method you would choose before calculating.

Answer probes: 'What did you already know that you leaned on?', 'How could you use what you already know to solve this?', 'Which fact helped, and why?', 'Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4 — why doesn't that change the answer?'
Compare cases: 'Could you solve 34 + 30 the same way? What changes?' and 'Would this splitting trick help for 34 + 9, or would you do something different there?'
Justify out loud which partition and which known bond you used.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing and justifying a strategy — recognising that partitioning preserves the total and that known facts can be scaled by place value — is the real mathematical work, beyond getting a single answer.

activities.title: Consolidation problems, including missing-number and trap items
feedback: For a dropped-unit choice (30 + 20 = 5), reconnect to blocks: twenty added to thirty is five tens, i.e. 50.
If a missing-number item is only attempted forwards, encourage testing values or using the bar model to work backwards from the whole (45) and the known part (10) to reach 35.
Ask the child to check the answer fits the problem's wording so an unreasonable result is questioned.
activities.rationale: Problem sets consolidate application and let specific misconceptions (dropping the unit, forwards-only thinking) be surfaced by targeted items, with a bar model making the missing-part structure visible. This format presents problems rather than coaching the forming strategy, so it suits practice after the strategy has been modelled.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
learnerActions: Solve missing-number and 'think of a number' problems (e.g. '__ + 10 = 45', 'I think of a number, add 10, and get 45 — what was my number?'), using a bar model to show the known part, the unknown part, and the whole.
Decide which partition would help a given problem before solving it.
Spot and reject the trap answer where the unit is dropped (e.g. recognise that 30 + 20 is 50, not 5).
Explain, for each item, which fact and which partition were used.
activities.intendedInsight: Place value and known facts can be applied across varied problem types, and keeping track of the unit (tens vs ones) is essential.

activities.title: Worked-example reference anchor
feedback: If a child treats the anchor as the only problem they can do, hand them a fresh problem and ask them to apply the same three steps — naming that deriving a new result is itself mathematics.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example is a useful reference for the structure of the strategy. Because problem-solving is generative, a single static example should be paired with new problems the child generates or attempts; it anchors rather than replaces practice.
learnerActions: Study one fully worked derived-fact chain (partition–operate–recombine on a single problem), revealing each step: split, operate on the relevant part, recombine.
Retell the steps in your own words before tackling a new problem of your own.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the full chain (e.g. 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54) gives a template children can imitate on new problems.

constraints: Keep the work strategy-based (partition–operate–recombine), not column-algorithm based, at this stage.
Always name the unit: a known bond like 3 + 2 scales to 30 + 20 = 50 only because these are tens; dropping the unit (saying 5) is the error to catch.
Partition correctly: 34 = 30 + 4, not 3 + 4 — the leading digit stands for tens.

Recognition/selection-only items (choosing which partition, spotting a trap answer) assess application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or spoken justification; pair them with building, writing, or explaining.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines, bar models) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
Insist on justification ('which fact? how did you split it?') so the META goal is assessed, not just the final answer.
A single static worked example cannot pose or respond to new problems; use it as an anchor alongside generative practice.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D format 'poor' claiming '3D adds nothing' and said a static image 'cannot pose or respond to new problems'; these catalog-style comparative claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal laws.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 34 + 20 = 54 and 30 + 20 = 50 are correct; the derived chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54 is consistent. Fresh examples check out: 34 + 30 = 64 and 56 + 20 = 76. The '30 + 20 = 5' statement appears only as a labelled misconception/distractor, never as a valid answer. The missing-number example '__ + 10 = 45' correctly resolves to 35.
The bar model (an original key representation for missing-number problems) is present in the consolidation/missing-number activity's learner actions, so the preservation claim is now accurate.
Both assessment error patterns are now reflected in feedback (the refusal/myth in the hands-on and anchor activities; defaulting to counting in the hands-on and Socratic activities).
Two source claims (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false in the row; retained verbatim only where they directly support a rationale, with no upgrade of their evidence status.

probeDeeper: What did you already know that you leaned on?
Could you solve 34 + 30 the same way? What changes?
Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4? Why doesn't that change the answer?
Would this splitting trick help for 34 + 9 too, or would you do something different there?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response reasons that you can split 34 into 30 and 4, use a fact you know (30 + 20 = 50), then recombine (50 + 4 = 54) — and can say why breaking a number up and leaning on known facts is a legitimate move.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes each calculation must be taught or memorised as its own item: 'I can't do it, we haven't done that one'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Think aloud how a known fact generates a new one; name derivation as real mathematics and invite the child to try building the next one themselves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child refuses to attempt an untaught combination or waits to be shown the method.

errorPatterns.pattern: Defaults to counting everything from one even when a known bond would shortcut the work
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the bonds — prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' so the known fact gets recruited; make the shortcut visible next to the count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child has the bonds but counts all 54 rather than recruiting 30 + 20.

responseLevels.gap: Insists the sum must be counted out or taught first; does not recruit any known fact.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously reasons that unfamiliar calculations can be derived by partitioning and leaning on known facts, and explains why partitioning preserves the total.
responseLevels.partial: Uses a known fact when prompted but treats it as a one-off, not as a general way to reach untaught answers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Here's 34 + 20. Suppose you'd never been shown this exact one before. Is there something you already know that could help you work it out without counting it all? Talk me through how you'd decide.' Surface the thinking for discussion — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe reveals the child's belief about where answers come from: whether calculations must be individually taught/memorised, or can be DERIVED from facts already held. That epistemic stance — not the single answer — is what is being surfaced.
